items.title: Lithium has a stronger 'urge' to react than sodium — and reacts more gently
items.claim: Drop sodium into water: it fizzes violently, often igniting with a yellow flame. Drop lithium into water: it floats and fizzes calmly. Yet lithium's standard electrode potential (-3.04 V) is MORE negative than sodium's (-2.71 V).
items.prompt: Why doesn't lithium react more vigorously?

options.text: Lithium's high melting point (181°C) means it stays solid during reaction; the LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms a coating that slows further reaction. Sodium melts in the reaction heat and exposes fresh surface
Standard electrode potentials are wrong for lithium
Lithium does not actually react with water

items.reveal:
Lithium's small ion has a very large hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs sodium's -406), which more than compensates for its higher ionisation energy. So thermodynamically it has the highest tendency in Group 1 to lose an electron in aqueous solution.

But reactivity at the bench is rate-controlled by surface kinetics. Sodium melts at 98°C, well below the temperature reached during reaction with water — molten sodium spreads and exposes fresh metal. Lithium melts at 181°C and stays solid.

LiOH solubility is about 12 g per 100 g water; NaOH is 109 g. The lithium product crusts on the surface and slows further attack.
items.why: The reactivity series is taught as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force and a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Gold is yellow because electrons travel near the speed of light
items.claim: Silver, copper and gold are all in Group 11 of the periodic table. Silver is shiny white, copper is reddish-orange, gold is yellow. The colour of gold is a relativistic effect — without Einstein, gold would look silver.

options.text: Gold absorbs light because it is the densest of the three

Gold's 1s electrons move at about 58 percent the speed of light, gaining relativistic mass; this contracts the s-orbitals, raises the 5d level and lowers the 6s level, shrinking the 5d-to-6s gap into the visible (blue absorbed, yellow reflected)
Gold's nucleus emits yellow light when irradiated
Gold's surface oxidises to give a yellow film

items.reveal:
For heavy elements, inner-shell electrons move at substantial fractions of c. Their relativistic mass increase contracts s and p orbitals, while shielded d and f orbitals expand.

For silver (Z=47) the effect is small — the 5s-to-4d transitions sit in the UV, so silver reflects all visible light evenly. For gold (Z=79) the effect is large — the 5d-to-6s transition slides into the visible blue region. Blue is absorbed; the complementary yellow is reflected.

Mercury's liquidity at room temperature has the same root cause: relativistic 6s contraction weakens mercury-mercury metallic bonding.
items.why: The colour of a metal is treated as a fixed elemental property. For heavy elements, it depends on special relativity.

items.title: Certain numbers of protons and neutrons make nuclei extra stable
items.claim: Helium-4, oxygen-16, calcium-40 and lead-208 are all unusually abundant and stable. They have 'magic numbers' of protons and/or neutrons: 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126.

options.text: Nuclei have a shell structure analogous to electron shells — completed proton or neutron shells confer extra binding energy and stability; this is the nuclear shell model
These numbers correspond to particle masses
They are leftover from the Big Bang

items.reveal:
Maria Goeppert-Mayer and J. Hans D. Jensen (1949) proposed that nucleons in a nucleus, like electrons in an atom, occupy quantum shells. Closed shells (magic numbers: 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) give exceptional binding energy.

Lead-208 is doubly magic (82 protons, 126 neutrons) — it is the heaviest stable nuclide. Oxygen-16 (8 and 8) and calcium-40 (20 and 20) are also doubly magic.

The search for an 'island of stability' near a hypothetical doubly magic superheavy nucleus (around Z=114, N=184) drives much modern heavy-element research. Goeppert-Mayer and Jensen shared the 1963 Nobel Prize.
items.why: Nuclear physics seems disconnected from quantum mechanics. The shell model says nuclei obey the same quantum-mechanical patterns as atoms — at a wildly different energy scale.
